nationality_or_literary_tradition: Kenyan; novelist, playwright, essayist and academic writing first in English and from the late 1970s in Gikuyu, in exile from the early 1980s, latterly in the United States
literary_identity: Kenyan novelist and theorist, East Africa's leading writer, whose Decolonising the Mind (1986) bade farewell to English and argued for African literatures in African languages
biography: Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o was born James Ngugi on 5 January 1938 in Kamiriithu, in the Kenya Colony. He studied at Makerere University and at the University of Leeds, and published his first novels in English, among them Weep Not, Child (1964), The River Between (1965), A Grain of Wheat (1967) and Petals of Blood (1977). In 1977 the play Ngaahika Ndeenda (I Will Marry When I Want), written with Ngũgĩ wa Mirii, was a commercial success but was shut down by the authoritarian government six weeks after it opened, and in December of that year he was imprisoned for more than a year; Amnesty International adopted him as a prisoner of conscience. After his release he turned to writing in Gikuyu and left Kenya. He taught at Yale, New York University and Northwestern, and became Distinguished Professor of Comparative Literature and English at the University of California, Irvine. In 1992 he founded the Gikuyu-language journal Mũtĩiri, which he edited until his death. He won the International Nonino Prize (2001) and the Park Kyong-ni Prize (2016), was often named for the Nobel Prize, and died on 28 May 2025 in Buford, Georgia.
literary_profile: His fiction runs from Weep Not, Child (1964) through A Grain of Wheat (1967) and Petals of Blood (1977) to the Gikuyu novels Matigari ma Njiruungi (1986) and Mũrogi wa Kagogo (Wizard of the Crow, 2006); his essays include Decolonising the Mind (1986).
stylistic_characteristics: Realist novels of the Mau Mau war and of independent Kenya that grow increasingly allegorical and satirical; participatory theatre; polemical, autobiographical essays.
intellectual_concerns: Colonialism and neocolonialism, land and class in Kenya, the Mau Mau rebellion, the betrayal of independence, and language as the carrier of culture and memory.
historical_significance: Described as East Africa's leading novelist and an important figure in modern African literature, and the most influential advocate of writing in African languages; Decolonising the Mind is one of the most cited texts of postcolonial studies.
bibliographical_notes: Installment 10, which records only Norton selections, holds Decolonising the Mind (1986). His novels, plays, stories, memoirs and other essays, named in Wikipedia's notable works (Weep Not, Child, 1964; The River Between, 1965; A Grain of Wheat, 1967; Petals of Blood, 1977; Matigari ma Njiruungi, 1986; Wizard of the Crow, 2006), have no work records, so the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Trinidad and Tobago-born Canadian; poet, novelist, essayist and playwright living in Toronto since the late 1960s
literary_identity: Caribbean-Canadian poet and former lawyer whose She Tries Her Tongue, Her Silence Softly Breaks (1989) and Zong! (2008) break and remake English to confront colonial and slave histories
biography: Marlene Nourbese Philip, usually credited as M. NourbeSe Philip, was born on 3 February 1947 in Woodlands, Moriah, on Tobago. She graduated from Bishop Anstey High School in 1965 and took a B.Sc. in economics at the University of the West Indies. Moving to Canada in 1968, she took graduate degrees in political science and law at the University of Western Ontario and practised law in Toronto for seven years, leaving the law in 1983 to write. She has published five books of poetry, two novels, four books of essays and two plays. The manuscript of She Tries Her Tongue, Her Silence Softly Breaks won the Casa de las Américas Prize; her novel Harriet's Daughter (1988) became a school text in Ontario and the Caribbean; and Zong! (2008), a poem cycle made from the legal report of the Zong massacre, has been performed in collective readings. She has held Guggenheim (1990) and MacDowell fellowships and received the PEN/Nabokov Award (2020), the Molson Prize (2021) and the Windham-Campbell Prize (2024).
literary_profile: Her poetry includes Thorns (1980), Salmon Courage (1983), She Tries Her Tongue, Her Silence Softly Breaks (1989) and Zong! (2008); her prose includes the novels Harriet's Daughter (1988) and Looking for Livingstone (1991) and the essays of Frontiers (1992), Genealogy of Resistance and Other Essays (1997) and Bla_k (2017).
stylistic_characteristics: Experimental, multi-voiced texts that fragment and collage English, set poems against prose, edicts and textbook language on the page, and play on etymology and sound; Caribbean demotic beside standard English.
intellectual_concerns: Language and silence; the mother tongue and the 'father tongue' imposed by colonialism and slavery; race, gender and the body; memory of the Middle Passage; social justice.
historical_significance: Widely taught and much studied for her experiments with form and her commitment to social justice; She Tries Her Tongue is her best-known book and 'Discourse on the Logic of Language' her most anthologised poem.
biographical_uncertainty: Wikipedia's infobox gives her birthplace as Woodlands, Moriah, Trinidad and Tobago, while its text says she was born in 'St. Ann, Jamaica'; the infobox is followed here, since she was schooled in Trinidad.
bibliographical_notes: Books (Wikipedia): poetry, Thorns (1980), Salmon Courage (1983), She Tries Her Tongue, Her Silence Softly Breaks (1989) and Zong! (2008); novels, Harriet's Daughter (1988) and Looking for Livingstone (1991); essays, Frontiers (1992), Showing Grit (1993), Caribana (1996), Genealogy of Resistance and Other Essays (1997) and Bla_k (2017); plays, Coups and Calypsos (1999) and Harriet's Daughter (2000). Installment 10, which records only Norton selections, holds 'Discourse on the Logic of Language' (1989); the books have no work records, so the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Indian-born British and American; novelist, short-story writer and essayist writing in English, in Britain from the 1960s and later in the United States (a citizen from 2016)
literary_identity: Indian-born novelist whose Midnight's Children (1981) remade the English novel of the subcontinent and whose The Satanic Verses (1988) brought a fatwa calling for his death
biography: Ahmed Salman Rushdie was born on 19 June 1947 in Bombay, in British India, two months before independence. He was educated at King's College, Cambridge, where he took a degree in history in 1968, and became a British citizen in 1964. His first novel, Grimus, appeared in 1975; his second, Midnight's Children (1981), won the Booker Prize and was later twice judged the best of all its winners. He wrote half a dozen pieces for the London Review of Books in its early years, among them the story 'The Prophet's Hair' (1981) and the essay 'Imaginary Homelands' (1982). After his fourth novel, The Satanic Verses (1988), Ayatollah Khomeini issued a fatwa calling for his death; the book was banned in twenty countries, and numerous killings and bombings were carried out by extremists who cited it. He was elected a fellow of the Royal Society of Literature in 1983 and knighted in 2007, and became an American citizen in 2016. In 2022 he survived a stabbing at the Chautauqua Institution that cost him the sight of his right eye.
literary_profile: His novels of the period include Grimus (1975), Midnight's Children (1981), Shame (1983), The Satanic Verses (1988), Haroun and the Sea of Stories (1990), The Moor's Last Sigh (1995) and The Ground Beneath Her Feet (1999); his essays are collected in Imaginary Homelands (1991) and his stories in East, West (1994).
stylistic_characteristics: Magical realism joined to historical fiction; exuberant, digressive, punning prose that mixes English with Hindustani and the idioms of Bombay; narrators who are self-conscious storytellers.
intellectual_concerns: Migration and the migrant as the defining figure of the century; the history of India and Pakistan after partition; religion, fanaticism and secularism; the freedom of the imagination and of speech; hybridity and the relations of East and West.
historical_significance: One of the most celebrated novelists of his generation; The Times ranked him thirteenth of the fifty greatest British writers since 1945, and the Satanic Verses affair made him a world symbol of the freedom to write.
bibliographical_notes: Installment 10, which records only Norton selections, holds 'The Prophet's Hair' (1981, collected in East, West, 1994) and Imaginary Homelands (1991), the essay collection from which Norton's two bracketed excerpts come. His novels, stories and other non-fiction have no work records. Titles of 1975-1999 named here beyond Midnight's Children and The Satanic Verses are general knowledge, not checked against a consulted bibliography; the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Guyanese; poet writing in English and in Guyanese Creole, resident in Britain since 1977
literary_identity: Guyanese-born poet of the Black British diaspora whose poems in Guyanese nation language and standard English give voice to the Middle Passage, the immigrant woman's body and the divided life of the Caribbean in Britain
biography: Grace Nichols was born in Georgetown, British Guiana, in 1950 and grew up in a village on the coast before her family moved to the city when she was eight. She took a diploma in communications at the University of Guyana and worked as a teacher from 1967 to 1970 and then as a journalist and in government information services. She migrated to Britain in 1977, the year her first pamphlet appeared, and worked as a teacher and freelance journalist in London. Her first collection, I is a Long-Memoried Woman (1983), a sequence spoken by an enslaved African woman, won the Commonwealth Poetry Prize, was dramatised for BBC radio and was filmed. The Fat Black Woman's Poems (1984) followed, then Lazy Thoughts of a Lazy Woman (1989), Sunris (1996), which won the Guyana Prize, and Startling the Flying Fish (2006). She has written novels, including Whole of a Morning Sky (1986), and many books for children, and edited anthologies of Caribbean women's poetry. Her partner is the poet John Agard. She was awarded the Queen's Gold Medal for Poetry in 2021 and lives in Lewes, East Sussex.
literary_profile: Poetry: I is a Long-Memoried Woman (1983), The Fat Black Woman's Poems (1984), Lazy Thoughts of a Lazy Woman (1989), Sunris (1996), Startling the Flying Fish (2006), Picasso, I Want My Face Back (2009), The Insomnia Poems (2017) and Passport to Here and There (2020); the retrospective I Have Crossed an Ocean: Selected Poems (2010). Fiction: Whole of a Morning Sky (1986). She has also published stories and poems for children and edited anthologies of Caribbean women's writing.
stylistic_characteristics: Short lyrics in mixed standard English and Guyanese Creole, using the rhythms of calypso and of Caribbean speech; stanza forms kept simple and firm; a comic, mocking extravagance (the Fat Black Woman poems) set against the elegiac and mythic sequences of the Middle Passage; frequent word-play across the two languages.
intellectual_concerns: Slavery, the Middle Passage and the survival of African culture in the Caribbean; migration, exile and the divided self of the Black British woman; the body, appetite and beauty against the standards of the metropolis; the Caribbean landscape and its folklore; mothers and daughters.
historical_significance: One of the central poets of Black British writing and a leading voice among the Caribbean writers who settled in Britain after the Windrush; her work is widely taught at GCSE and A level and has been recognised with the Commonwealth Poetry Prize (1983) and the Queen's Gold Medal for Poetry (2021).
bibliographical_notes: The list of books is taken from Wikipedia's bibliography and checked against the contents of I Have Crossed an Ocean: the collections I is a Long-Memoried Woman (Karnak House, 1983), The Fat Black Woman's Poems (Virago, 1984), Lazy Thoughts of a Lazy Woman (Virago, 1989), Sunris (Virago, 1996) and Startling the Flying Fish (2006), with the later Picasso, I Want My Face Back (Bloodaxe, 2009), The Insomnia Poems (2017) and Passport to Here and There (Bloodaxe, 2020). None of these books has a work record: installment 10 records only the three Norton selections, 'Epilogue' (1983), 'The Fat Black Woman Goes Shopping' (1984) and 'Wherever I Hang' (1989), so the bibliography of the author's books is incomplete. Her children's books were not checked title by title.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Jamaican; dub poet and recording artist, resident in Britain since 1963, writing in Jamaican Creole and English
literary_identity: Jamaican-born dub poet of Brixton whose verse in Jamaican Creole, performed over reggae and collected in slim books, is the most influential body of British performance poetry of the late twentieth century
biography: Linton Kwesi Johnson was born on 24 August 1952 in Chapelton, Clarendon, in rural Jamaica, and joined his mother in Brixton, south London, in 1963. He attended Tulse Hill School, joined the British Black Panther movement while still at school, and studied sociology at Goldsmiths College, graduating in 1973. He worked as the first paid library resources and education officer at the Keskidee Centre, the black arts centre in Islington, and wrote for the music papers. His poems appeared in the journal Race Today, which published his first collection, Voices of the Living and the Dead (1974), followed by Dread Beat an' Blood (Bogle-L'Ouverture, 1975) and Inglan Is a Bitch (Race Today, 1980); he also recorded the poems with the dub band of the producer Dennis Bovell, on albums including Dread Beat an' Blood (1978), Forces of Victory (1979) and Bass Culture (1980). He founded LKJ Records in 1981. Mi Revalueshanary Fren: Selected Poems (Penguin Modern Classics, 2002) made him one of the few living poets in the series, and his essays were collected in Time Come (2023). He holds the Jamaican Order of Distinction, was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society of Literature in 2013, and won the PEN Pinter Prize in 2020.
literary_profile: Poetry: Voices of the Living and the Dead (1974), Dread Beat an' Blood (1975), Inglan Is a Bitch (1980), Tings an Times: Selected Poems (1991) and Mi Revalueshanary Fren: Selected Poems (2002). Criticism and prose: Time Come: Selected Prose (2023). Records: Dread Beat an' Blood (1978), Forces of Victory (1979), Bass Culture (1980), LKJ in Dub (1980) and Making History (1983).
stylistic_characteristics: Poems written for performance in Jamaican Creole ('nation language'), with a strong stress beat, refrain and repetition; the diction is a transcription of the spoken language, unpunctuated in places and shaped for the voice; the printed texts stand as poems but assume the bass line of reggae behind them.
intellectual_concerns: Racial oppression and police violence in Britain; the daily exploitation of Black labour ('Inglan Is a Bitch'); the Brixton uprisings and the Black British struggle of the 1970s and 1980s; migration and belonging; solidarity, mourning and memorial.
historical_significance: The founder of British dub poetry and the model for a generation of performance poets, from Jean 'Binta' Breeze to Benjamin Zephaniah; his records carried the poems to a mass audience and his work is credited as a precursor of rap. 'Inglan Is a Bitch' became an emblem of Black British experience in the Thatcher years.
bibliographical_notes: Books, from Wikipedia and the OpenEdition study of his work: Voices of the Living and the Dead (1974), Dread Beat an' Blood (Bogle-L'Ouverture, 1975), Inglan Is a Bitch (Race Today, 1980), Tings an Times (1991) and Mi Revalueshanary Fren (Penguin, 2002), with the prose collection Time Come (2023). Only the Norton selection, 'Inglan Is a Bitch' (1980), has a work record, so the bibliography is incomplete; the albums were not checked title by title and have no records.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British (born in Persia, raised in Southern Rhodesia); novelist, short-story writer and essayist
literary_identity: Nobel laureate and one of the great novelists of postwar Britain, whose sequence of novels and stories from The Grass Is Singing to The Golden Notebook and the Canopus in Argos series tested the forms of realism, autobiography and speculative fiction against the politics of gender, race and empire
biography: Doris May Tayler was born on 22 October 1919 in Kermanshah, Persia, where her father, a former bank clerk crippled in the First World War, worked for the Imperial Bank of Persia; her mother had been a nurse. The family moved to Southern Rhodesia in 1925 and she grew up on a farm near Salisbury, educated at a convent school and then, briefly, in Salisbury, leaving school at fourteen. She married Frank Wisdom in 1939, had two children, and divorced in 1943; a second marriage, to the German communist Gottfried Lessing, ended in 1949. She had joined the Communist Party in Rhodesia and brought the manuscript of her first novel to London in 1949. The Grass Is Singing appeared in 1950, followed by the five novels of Children of Violence (1952-1969), The Golden Notebook (1962), Briefing for a Descent into Hell (1971), the five Canopus in Argos: Archives novels (1979-1983), The Good Terrorist (1985), The Fifth Child (1988) and, late, Love, Again (1996) and Alfred and Emily (2008). She wrote more than seventy books, including the stories of African Stories, A Man and Two Women and To Room Nineteen, the memoir Under My Skin (1994) and the essays of A Small Personal Voice and Prisons We Choose to Live Inside. She was awarded the David Cohen Prize in 2001 and the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2007. She died in London on 17 November 2013.
literary_profile: Novels: The Grass Is Singing (1950), Children of Violence (Martha Quest, 1952; A Proper Marriage, 1954; A Ripple from the Storm, 1958; Landlocked, 1965; The Four-Gated City, 1969), The Golden Notebook (1962), Briefing for a Descent into Hell (1971), The Summer Before the Dark (1973), The Memoirs of a Survivor (1974), Canopus in Argos: Archives (Shikasta, 1979; The Marriages Between Zones Three, Four and Five, 1980; The Sirian Experiments, 1981; The Making of the Representative for Planet 8, 1982; Documents Relating to the Sentimental Agents in the Volyen Empire, 1983), The Diary of a Good Neighbour (1983, as Jane Somers), If the Old Could (1984), The Good Terrorist (1985), The Fifth Child (1988), Love, Again (1996), Mara and Dann (1999), Ben, in the World (2000), The Sweetest Dream (2001), The Cleft (2007) and Alfred and Emily (2008). Stories: This Was the Old Chief's Country (1951), Five (1953), The Habit of Loving (1957), A Man and Two Women (1963), African Stories (1964), The Story of a Non-Marrying Man (1972), To Room Nineteen: Collected Stories Volume One (1978) and The Temptation of Jack Orkney (1978). Nonfiction: Going Home (1957), In Pursuit of the English (1960), Particularly Cats (1967), A Small Personal Voice (1974), Prisons We Choose to Live Inside (1987), The Wind Blows Away Our Words (1987), African Laughter (1992) and Under My Skin (1994).
stylistic_characteristics: From the strict realism of the early African novels and stories to the four-column notebook of The Golden Notebook, Lessing kept changing form: documentary realism, interior monologue, Sufi allegory, space fiction, horror and late fable. The prose is plain and fast, with a strong narrative pull, and she uses the short story as a clinical instrument for exposing the ordinary arrangements of marriage and class.
intellectual_concerns: The position of women, marriage and the search for a free self (the 'free women' of The Golden Notebook, Susan Rawlings in 'To Room Nineteen'); colonialism and racial guilt in southern Africa; communism and political disillusion; madness and breakdown as the price of conformity; the survival of the species (the Canopus novels, The Memoirs of a Survivor); Sufism and the idea of a higher order.
historical_significance: The most important British novelist of the second half of the twentieth century to write from a colonial background, and with The Golden Notebook a founding text of the second wave of feminism, although Lessing resisted the label. The Nobel citation praised 'that epicist of the female experience, who with scepticism, fire and visionary power has subjected a divided civilisation to scrutiny'.
bibliographical_notes: The list of books is taken from Wikipedia and from general knowledge and has not been checked title by title against a bibliography; the dates are those of first British publication. Installment 10 records only the Norton selection, 'To Room Nineteen' (1963), so the author's bibliography is incomplete. The five volumes of Children of Violence are listed with their individual titles, but with no work records.

birthplace: Mysore, Kingdom of Mysore (now Karnataka), India
nationality_or_literary_tradition: Indian; poet, translator, linguist and folklorist, professor at the University of Chicago from 1962
literary_identity: Indian poet and scholar who wrote a small, exact body of English poems on family, body and memory and transformed the study and translation of classical Tamil and Kannada into English
biography: Attipate Krishnaswami Ramanujan was born in Mysore on 16 March 1929, the son of a professor of mathematics and astrologer, and was educated at Marimallappa's High School and the Maharaja College of Mysore, where he read English. He taught English at colleges in Quilon, Belgaum and Baroda, and went in 1959 to Indiana University as a Fulbright scholar, taking a doctorate in linguistics in 1963. In 1962 he joined the University of Chicago, where he spent the rest of his career in the departments of South Asian Languages and Civilizations and of Linguistics and on the Committee on Social Thought, becoming the William E. Colvin Professor. His first collection, The Striders (1966), was followed by Relations (1971), Selected Poems (1976) and Second Sight (1986); The Collected Poems appeared in 1995, with poems for a further volume, The Black Hen. As a translator and scholar he published The Interior Landscape: Love Poems from a Classical Tamil Anthology (1967), Speaking of Siva (1973), Hymns for the Drowning (1981), Poems of Love and War (1985), Folktales from India (1991) and, with Velcheru Narayana Rao and David Shulman, When God Is a Customer (1994); his essays include 'Is There an Indian Way of Thinking?' (1990) and 'Three Hundred Ramayanas' (1991). He was awarded the Padma Shri in 1976 and a MacArthur Fellowship in 1983. He died in Chicago on 13 July 1993, of a reaction to anaesthesia before surgery; the Sahitya Akademi Award came posthumously, in 1999, for The Collected Poems.
literary_profile: Poetry: The Striders (London: Oxford University Press, 1966), Relations (1971), Selected Poems (1976), Second Sight (1986) and The Collected Poems (1995, with The Black Hen). Translations and studies: The Interior Landscape (1967), Speaking of Siva (1973), Hymns for the Drowning (1981), Poems of Love and War (1985), Folktales from India (1991) and When God Is a Customer (1994). Essays: 'Is There an Indian Way of Thinking?' (1990) and 'Three Hundred Ramayanas' (1991).
stylistic_characteristics: Short free-verse lyrics in a spare, exact, often epigrammatic English; a poetry of lists, definitions and catalogues ('Elements of Composition' composes the self out of chemical elements); colloquial speech as a dramatic resource; the classical Tamil and Kannada metres of his translations carried over into his own line.
intellectual_concerns: Family resemblance and inheritance (the father's signature on a stranger's face); the body as a compound of earth, air, fire and water; the divided self of the Indian who lives in two languages; death, memory and the minute particulars of ordinary life; folklore and myth as living structures.
historical_significance: The founding figure of Indian English poetry's second generation, who made the Indian-English lyric out of speech rather than imperial rhetoric; as a translator he changed the English reading of classical Tamil, and as a folklorist he helped establish the study of Indian oral narrative.
bibliographical_notes: The books are listed from Wikipedia and from the Oxford University Press and Selected Poetry materials, and checked against the contents of The Striders (1966) and Second Sight (1986). Only the two Norton selections, 'Self-Portrait' (1966) and 'Elements of Composition' (1986), have work records, so the bibliography is incomplete; the translations and scholarly books have no records, and the posthumous The Black Hen was not checked in detail.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; poet resident in the United States from 1954, writing in English
literary_identity: English poet of The Movement who moved to California, wrote some of the finest formal verse of his generation and then, in The Man with Night Sweats, the defining English elegies of the AIDS epidemic
biography: Thomson William Gunn was born on 29 August 1929 in Gravesend, Kent, the son of two journalists; his parents divorced when he was ten and his mother, who had taught him to read poetry, killed herself when he was a teenager. He was educated at University College School in Hampstead and read English at Trinity College, Cambridge, graduating in 1953. His first collection, Fighting Terms, appeared in 1954 from the Fantasy Press, and in the same year he moved to the United States to teach at Stanford and to be with Michael Kitay, his partner for the rest of his life. He taught at Berkeley from 1958 to 1966 and again from 1973 to 2000. The Sense of Movement (1957) confirmed him as a poet of The Movement, but Touch (1967), with its free verse and its frank poems of gay life, began the change that Moly (1971), Jack Straw's Castle (1976) and The Passages of Joy (1982) carried through. The Man with Night Sweats (1992), written as his friends died of AIDS, won the Lenore Marshall Poetry Prize, and Boss Cupid (2000) was his last collection. He also published two books of essays, The Occasions of Poetry (1982) and Shelf Life (1993), and received the David Cohen Prize in 2003. He died in San Francisco on 25 April 2004.
literary_profile: Poetry: Fighting Terms (1954), The Sense of Movement (1957), My Sad Captains and Other Poems (1961), Touch (1967), Moly (1971), Jack Straw's Castle (1976), The Passages of Joy (1982), The Man with Night Sweats (1992) and Boss Cupid (2000); Selected Poems 1950-1975 (1979) and Collected Poems (1993). Prose: The Occasions of Poetry (1982) and Shelf Life (1993).
stylistic_characteristics: Early poems in tight stanza forms and strict metre, with a clipped, muscular syntax and a taste for the dramatic situation; the later work opens into syllabics and free verse without losing its measure; the AIDS elegies return to plain quatrains and iambic pentameter; a persistent concern with the body, surfaces and contact.
intellectual_concerns: Energy, violence and the will (the early poems of motorcycles, gangs and soldiers); drug-taking, sex and the bohemian life of San Francisco; friendship, loss and the AIDS epidemic (The Man with Night Sweats); balance, surfing and the discipline of form as an image of how to live; the meeting of English and American poetry.
historical_significance: The most formally accomplished poet of The Movement after Larkin, and the one who remade himself most radically; The Man with Night Sweats is the central book of AIDS elegies in English and is credited with restoring poetry to a public role in the crisis.
bibliographical_notes: Books, from Wikipedia and the WorldCat contents of Collected Poems: Fighting Terms (1954), The Sense of Movement (1957), My Sad Captains and Other Poems (1961), Touch (1967), Moly (1971), Jack Straw's Castle (1976), The Passages of Joy (1982), The Man with Night Sweats (1992) and Boss Cupid (2000). Installment 10 records only the five Norton selections ('Black Jackets' and 'My Sad Captains', 1961; 'From the Wave', 1971; 'Still Life' and 'The Missing', 1992), so the bibliography is incomplete; the essay collections have no records.
